title: Two independent semilocal rings give an affine intersection cover
statement: Let $K$ be a field [def-weil-field] and let $C,D\subseteq K$ be unital subrings with fraction field $K$. Assume that both rings are Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], semilocal (have finitely many maximal ideals), and of Krull dimension exactly one [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Suppose the multiplication map $C\otimes_{\mathbb Z}D\to K$ is surjective [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Put $R=C\cap D$. Then the inclusions induce open immersions $\operatorname{Spec}C\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ and $\operatorname{Spec}D\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-open-immersion] whose images cover $\operatorname{Spec}R$. Moreover the multiplication map $C\otimes_R D\to K$ is an isomorphism of rings.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sc-jacobson-denominator-function-field] with $A=C$ and the singleton family $B_1=D$. Obtain $0\ne f\in C$ with $t=f^{-1}\in\operatorname{Jac}(D)$, where $\operatorname{Jac}$ denotes the intersection of all maximal ideals. Apply it again with $A=D$, $B_1=C$ to obtain $0\ne g\in D$ with $s=g^{-1}\in\operatorname{Jac}(C)$. All its Noetherian, dimension-one, semilocal and common-fraction-field hypotheses are exactly the assumptions here. The second tensor map is surjective because swapping pure tensors gives an inverse pair of linear maps $C\otimes_{\mathbb Z}D\leftrightarrow D\otimes_{\mathbb Z}C$, by the universal property and generation by pure tensors [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]; multiplication into $K$ is unchanged.

source.place: Tag 09N5 (varieties-lemma-create-globally-generated), applied twice with a singleton family; agent assembly for Tag 09N3 (varieties-lemma-semi-local-both-side).

proof.text: Put $a=fs\in\operatorname{Jac}(C)$ and $b=gt\in\operatorname{Jac}(D)$; then $ab=1$ in $K$. The Jacobson radicals are ideals, being intersections of ideals. By [lem-weil-pbc-jacobson-radical-one-plus-units] applied to those ideals, $1+a$ is a unit of $C$ and $1+b$ a unit of $D$. Define $x=(1+a)^{-1}$ and $y=a(1+a)^{-1}$ in $K$. Since $ab=1$, $x=b(1+b)^{-1}$ and $y=(1+b)^{-1}$. The first formulas show $x\in C^\times$ and $y\in\operatorname{Jac}(C)$; the second show $x\in\operatorname{Jac}(D)$ and $y\in D^\times$. Thus $x,y\in R=C\cap D$, both are nonzero, and $x+y=1$.

source.place: Tag 0AME (algebra-lemma-contained-in-radical), equivalence (1) and (2); explicit reciprocal-element calculation supplied by the agent.

proof.text: For each pair $(B,h)=(C,y)$ or $(D,x)$, prove $B_h=K$ using [def-weil-ring-localization-away]. Let $0\ne d\in B$. Every prime $\mathfrak p$ containing $d$ is nonzero. It is contained in a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-ideal-contained-in-maximal]; if $\mathfrak p\subsetneq\mathfrak m$, the chain $(0)\subsetneq\mathfrak p\subsetneq\mathfrak m$ contradicts $\dim B=1$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Hence every such prime is maximal and contains $h\in\operatorname{Jac}(B)$. By the radical-intersection clause of [lem-weil-pbc-zero-locus-eq-iff-radical-eq], $h\in\sqrt{(d)}$. Thus $h^n=de$ for some $n\ge1$ and $e\in B$, so $d^{-1}=e/h^n\in B_h$. Every element of the fraction field $K$ is therefore in $B_h$. The fraction map $B_h\to K$ is injective: $h\ne0$ and a fraction mapping to zero has zero numerator in the domain $B$. This identifies the rings inside $K$.

source.place: Tag 00E0 (algebra-lemma-Zariski-topology), items (2) and (7), and Definition 00KE (algebra-definition-Krull); applied to the two radical elements constructed above.

proof.text: Since $x$ is a unit of $C$, the fractions $r/x^n$ with $r\in R$ lie in $C$. Conversely, for $c\in C\subset K=D_x$ write $c=d/x^n$ with $d\in D$ and $n\ge0$. Then $d=x^nc\in C$ as $x,c\in C$, so $d\in C\cap D=R$. Thus $C=R_x$ inside $K$. Likewise $y$ is a unit of $D$ and $K=C_y$; for $d\in D$ write $d=c/y^n$, whence $c=y^nd\in D\cap C=R$. Thus $D=R_y$. These are identifications over $R$, with injectivity checked by the zero-numerator criterion for localization fractions [def-weil-ring-localization-away].

source.place: Tag 09N3 (varieties-lemma-semi-local-both-side), final paragraph: the principal-localization conclusion; explicit denominator argument using the two witnesses from Tag 09N5.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-principal-localization-open-immersion] to $R_x$ and $R_y$. Under the identifications in Step 4, the resulting morphisms are precisely the morphisms induced by the inclusions $R\subset C,D$, and they are open immersions with images $D_R(x)$ and $D_R(y)$. These images cover: a prime of $R$ outside both would contain $x$ and $y$, hence $x+y=1$, contrary to being proper. Here $D_R(h)$ denotes the primes not containing $h$, as in the cited statement.

source.place: Tag 01I3 (schemes-lemma-standard-open-affine), proof identifying Spec of a principal localization with its basic open; cover checked by x+y=1.

proof.text: Apply the module clause of [lem-weil-pbc-localization-tensor] to the $R$-module $D$ and the element $x\in R$. It gives a bijective linear map $R_x\otimes_R D\to D_x$, $(r/x^n)\otimes d\mapsto rd/x^n$. Steps 3 and 4 identify its source with $C\otimes_R D$ and its target with $K$. On each pure tensor $c\otimes d$ its value is $cd\in K$, so it equals the multiplication map in the statement by generation by pure tensors [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. That ring homomorphism is therefore bijective, hence an isomorphism of rings.

source.place: Tag 00DK (algebra-lemma-tensor-localization), formula for the canonical module isomorphism; specialized to powers of x and M=D.
